source_document.body:
Artificial intelligence doesn’t need to control a warehouse or predict a major disruption to be useful. Those in the supply chain industry can use AI tools to handle many of the smaller tasks that fill their days.
What’s Related
Tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can organize information, suggest questions, draft routine documents and provide a starting point for analysis . However, they can’t guarantee their answers are complete or correct. Someone who understands the business and the decision being made should review every AI response.
The following examples show where AI can help with everyday supply chain work. Each includes a sample prompt and the checks users should make before relying on the response.
1. Compare Supplier Bids
What AI can do: AI can organize bids into a common format and highlight differences in price, delivery times, payment terms, minimum orders, and other requirements. It can also identify questions that need answering before selecting a supplier.
Sample prompt: “Compare these three supplier proposals. Create a table showing price, delivery time, payment terms, minimum order quantity, contract length, and any added fees. Then list five questions I should ask before making a decision.”
What information to provide: Include the same categories of information for every supplier. Tell the AI which factors matter most and whether any requirements are mandatory.
What to double-check: Verify every price, date, fee, and contract term against the original proposals. AI may overlook important differences or place too much weight on the wrong factors.
RELATED: 40 ChatGPT Prompts Every Supply Chain Professional Should Know
2. Draft a Request for Proposal
What AI can do: AI can draft a request for proposal, or RFP, based on a company’s shipping , warehousing , technology or purchasing needs. It can also suggest questions for potential vendors.
Sample prompt: “Draft an RFP for a company seeking a new regional parcel carrier . Include sections covering service area, pricing, delivery times, tracking, claims, peak-season charges, customer support, and implementation.”
What information to provide: Explain what is being purchased, expected shipment or order volume, service requirements, deadlines, and the information vendors must submit.
What to double-check: Make sure the document includes all business, legal, security and service requirements. Purchasing and legal teams should review it before it’s sent to vendors.
Prompts for other parts of the job
“What should I look at first if put-away times suddenly spike?”
“Explain why transportation costs jump during peak season in simple terms.”
“Draft a response to a customer asking why their order is delayed. Professional but empathetic.”
“Turn this table into a short narrative I can use in a leadership update.”
“What happens if our main supplier can’t ship for 30 days?”
“Explain Scope 3 emissions in plain language.”
“Create a one-page cheat sheet on inbound vs. outbound logistics.”
“Rewrite this email so it’s shorter and more direct.”
3. Review Shipment Exceptions
What AI can do: AI can sort a list of late, damaged, or stalled shipments and group them by carrier, customer, location, product, or reason for the exception. It can then summarize which problems appear most often.
Sample prompt: “Review this shipment exception report. Group the problems by carrier and reason, identify the most common issues, and list the shipments that require immediate attention.”
What information to provide: Include shipment status, promised delivery date, carrier, origin, destination, customer priority and the reason for each exception. Remove customer names and other restricted information unless the tool is approved for that data.
What to double-check: Confirm that urgent shipments weren’t missed. Always compare the AI’s summary with the original report before anyone contacts a carrier or customer.
4. Find Patterns in Inventory Data
What AI can do: When used with an approved tool that can read spreadsheets, AI can help identify slow-moving inventory , frequent stockouts, unusual changes in demand, and products that may need further review.
Sample prompt: “Analyze this inventory spreadsheet. Identify products with more than 90 days of supply, items that stocked out more than twice, and any large changes in weekly demand. Explain how you reached each conclusion.”
What information to provide: Include product numbers, inventory levels, order history, sales or usage data, lead times, and the period covered by the file. Define terms such as “slow-moving” or “stockout.”
What to double-check: Review the formulas, date ranges, units of measurement, and assumptions. AI can misread spreadsheet columns or treat missing information as zero.
5. Turn an SOP Into a Checklist
What AI can do: AI can convert a lengthy standard operating procedure into a shorter checklist for receiving, picking , packing, loading, equipment inspections, or other repeatable work.
Sample prompt: “Turn this receiving procedure into a step-by-step checklist for warehouse employees. Keep every required safety and quality check, use plain language, and flag any instruction that is unclear.”
What information to provide: Give the AI the current approved procedure and explain who will use the checklist. Include any steps that must be completed in a set order.
What to double-check: Make sure no safety, regulatory, or quality-control step was removed. A supervisor should test the checklist against the full procedure before it’s used.
6. Prepare for a Supplier Meeting
What AI can do: AI can turn performance data and past meeting notes into a proposed agenda. It can also suggest questions about late deliveries, quality problems, pricing changes, or upcoming orders.
Sample prompt: “Using these supplier scorecard results and meeting notes, create a 30-minute meeting agenda. Include questions about late deliveries, rejected orders, corrective actions, and expected demand next quarter.”
What information to provide: Share approved performance figures, open problems, previous commitments, and the goal of the meeting. Describe the supplier relationship and the decisions that need to be made.
What to double-check: Confirm that the questions reflect current information. AI doesn’t know about phone calls, emails or agreements not included in the prompt.
7. Draft Routine Supplier or Customer Messages
What AI can do: AI can draft an email about a delayed order, missing paperwork, a scheduling change, a price request or another common issue. It can also adjust the wording to make a message clearer or less confrontational.
Sample prompt: “Draft a direct but professional email to a supplier about an order that is five days late. Ask for the current status, the reason for the delay, a confirmed delivery date, and steps to prevent another delay.”
What information to provide: Explain what happened, what has already been discussed, what response is needed, and when it’s needed. Avoid adding private contact or account information to an unapproved tool.
What to double-check: Review names, dates, order numbers, commitments, and tone. Never allow AI to send the message automatically without a person reviewing it.
8. Explain an Unfamiliar Supply Chain Term
What AI can do: AI can explain a shipping term, contract provision, warehouse metric, trade document or industry acronym in plain language. It can also give a simple example showing how the term is used.
Sample prompt: “Explain demurrage and detention in plain language. Describe the difference between them, give one example of each, and explain why a shipper might be charged.”
What information to provide: Name the term and provide any relevant context, such as ocean shipping, trucking , procurement or warehousing. Ask the tool to identify anything that may differ by carrier, country, or contract.
What to double-check: Confirm definitions with a trusted source. Trade rules, contracts, fees, and government requirements can change, and an AI tool may provide outdated information.
9. Build Demand-Planning Scenarios
What AI can do: AI can help planners outline possible high-, medium-, and low-demand scenarios. It can suggest questions to consider when sales, supplier lead times, promotions or economic conditions change.
Sample prompt: “Create three demand scenarios for the next quarter using sales estimates of 8,000, 10,000, and 12,000 units. For each scenario, list the inventory, supplier, warehouse, and transportation questions the planning team should review.”
What information to provide: Include the forecast period, expected demand, current inventory, lead times, order limits, promotions, and known business constraints.
What to double-check: Treat the output as a planning aid, not a forecast. AI-generated scenarios shouldn’t replace the company’s demand data, planning system, or the judgment of employees who understand the market.
10. Investigate a Recurring Supply Chain Problem
What AI can do: AI can organize known facts about recurring delays, shortages, picking errors or quality problems. It can suggest possible causes and help create a list of questions for a root-cause review.
Sample prompt: “These orders were shipped late during the past four weeks. Group the incidents by product, shift, day, and reason. Suggest possible causes to investigate, but separate confirmed facts from assumptions.”
What information to provide: Include dates, locations, products, work shifts, systems involved, reported causes, and any recent changes. Clearly distinguish known facts from employee opinions.
What to double-check: Don’t assume the suggested causes are correct. AI can identify patterns, but employees must examine the process, speak with the people involved, and confirm what actually happened.

The Department of Energy (DOE) has offered Constellation Energy a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion to finance nuclear power uprates and modernization at eight plants in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. The proposed investments could add nearly 1.1 GW of generating capacity to the nation’s existing nuclear fleet.
The commitment marks the agency’s second major nuclear uprate financing offer this month and is poised to advance its Utility Power Reactor Incremental Scaling Effort (UPRISE) , which has now identified approximately 4.7 GW of potential nuclear capacity additions toward a 5-GW target.
The DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) announced the commitment on Oct. 27 during Energy Secretary Chris Wright’s visit to Constellation’s Byron Generating Station in Illinois. The financing would support potential uprates at eight nuclear plants comprising 15 operating reactors, representing approximately 15.5 GW of net generating capacity attributable to Constellation’s ownership interests, according to its 2025 annual report .
The proposed EDF financing portfolio includes three pressurized water reactor (PWR) facilities, comprising six reactors: Braidwood (2,386 MW) and Byron (2,350 MW) in Illinois, and Calvert Cliffs (1,789 MW) in Maryland. The remaining five facilities operate nine boiling water reactors (BWRs): Clinton (1,092 MW), Dresden (1,845 MW), LaSalle (2,320 MW), and Quad Cities (1,403 MW) in Illinois, and Limerick (2,315 MW) in Pennsylvania. Constellation, notably, owns 75% of Quad Cities.
The proposed investments are geared to expand nuclear output across the PJM Interconnection and Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) regions, where DOE suggested additional generation would strengthen grid reliability. Both regions have faced reliability pressures that prompted DOE emergency orders this year. Most recently, on Oct. 12, DOE authorized PJM to dispatch additional generation as needed amid elevated maintenance outages and tightening reserve margins. The agency has also ordered several fossil-fired plants in the two regions to remain available, including Constellation’s Eddystone units in Pennsylvania.
However, the proposed nuclear uprates would provide longer-term capacity additions. Constellation’s previously announced Google-backed projects are expected to begin delivering additional capacity in 2028 and be completed by the end of 2032. Its Amazon-backed uprate at Calvert Cliffs is scheduled for 2030 to 2032.
DOE said the commitment also includes an option to finance additional uprate projects at other Constellation facilities. However, the agency cautioned: “While this conditional commitment indicates DOE’s intent to provide a loan, Constellation must satisfy certain technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before the Department enters into definitive financing documents and funds the loan.” Separately, Constellation emphasized that the commitment does not constitute a final investment decision for any individual uprate or guarantee that projects will proceed at every facility under consideration.
Federal Financing Builds on Constellation’s Customer-Backed Nuclear Uprates
The conditional loan commitment could provide an additional source of financing for Constellation’s expanding nuclear uprate program, which is already supported by multibillion-dollar investments tied to long-term electricity purchase agreements with major technology companies.
In its Oct. 27 announcement , Constellation said its recent 20-year agreements with Google and Amazon have incentivized more than $7 billion in investments to add approximately 1,080 MW of nuclear generating capacity. A separate agreement with Meta, announced in 2025, supports a 30-MW expansion at Clinton in Illinois.
The commercial arrangements provide long-term revenue certainty for investments that would increase electrical output from existing reactors. Constellation has said the proposed federal financing could reduce borrowing costs and potentially accelerate development or support a broader portfolio of projects.
“This is how America wins the race for energy abundance – by pairing private-sector demand and investment with smart federal financing to unlock more power from the nuclear plants we already have,” said Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s chairman, president, and CEO. “Our agreements with Google and Amazon demonstrate how long-term customer commitments can incentivize billions of dollars in investment in new, reliable nuclear capacity. This conditional loan commitment can help us move faster and go further, putting more reliable power on the grid, creating and preserving good-paying jobs, strengthening American energy security and helping families and businesses manage energy costs.”
As POWER reported on Oct. 7 , Google’s 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) supports approximately $4.3 billion of investments to add 890 MW at 11 nuclear units across six sites in PJM. The proposed upgrades would increase thermal and electrical efficiency through equipment modernization, including improvements to turbines, steam-cycle systems, and plant controls.
The six facilities previously identified as likely participants in the Google agreement were Braidwood, Byron, LaSalle, Quad Cities, and Limerick, along with Salem in New Jersey. Five are included in DOE’s newly announced financing portfolio. Salem, which is operated by PSEG and in which Constellation holds a 42.59% ownership interest, is not on the DOE list. However, Constellation has not publicly confirmed how Google’s 890 MW will be distributed among the participating reactors.
The DOE portfolio also includes facilities associated with other customer agreements. Amazon’s 20-year PPA supports an approximately 190-MW expansion at Calvert Cliffs, while Meta’s agreement underpins 30 MW of additional capacity at Clinton. Dresden is covered by a 176-MW agreement with Walmart that includes 30 MW of planned uprates.
The scope of the proposed federal financing, for now, remains unclear, particularly given its overlap with Constellation’s existing customer-backed uprate commitments.
The proposed uprates would entail varying degrees of engineering modifications and Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) licensing requirements, depending on reactor design, existing equipment, and the scope of each capacity increase. As POWER previously reported , UPRISE encompasses operational and balance-of-plant improvements, measurement uncertainty recapture (MUR) uprates, and more extensive power uprates that can increase licensed reactor thermal power by as much as 20%.
According to the NRC’s expected-applications list , updated Sept. 8, Constellation is expected to submit 12 power uprate applications between the fourth quarter of 2026 and the end of 2030, including five extended power uprates (EPUs) and seven MUR uprates. However, the NRC lists the individual plants as proprietary, so the anticipated applications cannot yet be matched to the eight facilities covered by DOE’s conditional financing commitment.
DOE’s Nuclear Uprate Financing Push Expands
Constellation’s conditional commitment follows a similar Oct. 5 offer to Vistra of up to $4.2 billion for uprates and modernization at Beaver Valley (1,872 MW) in Pennsylvania and Davis-Besse (908 MW) and Perry (1,268 MW) in Ohio. DOE said the projects could add 433 MW of nuclear capacity while preserving more than 4 GW of existing generation. The planned uprates comprise 213 MW at Perry, 80 MW at Davis-Besse, and 70 MW at each of Beaver Valley’s two reactors.
As POWER previously reported, Vistra plans combined EPUs and MUR improvements across all four reactors, targeting thermal power increases of 16% at Perry, 6.9% at Beaver Valley, and 7% at Davis-Besse. Perry’s modifications could include a new cooling tower and major turbine-generator upgrades. The projects are supported by 20-year PPAs with Meta, which will purchase the additional output along with approximately 2.18 GW of existing generation from Perry and Davis-Besse. Vistra expects the uprates to enter service between 2031 and 2034.
Combined, the Constellation and Vistra conditional loan commitments total up to $9.2 billion and could support approximately 1.5 GW of additional nuclear capacity. Neither financing package has been finalized yet, however.
DOE has also advanced nuclear uprate financing through a broader $26.5 billion loan package closed with Southern Co. in February . That financing is slated to support projects across Georgia Power and Alabama Power, including nuclear generation upgrades and license renewals, as well as natural gas generation, hydropower modernization, and transmission improvements.
Under the package, EDF initiated federal historic-preservation consultations on Sept. 1 for proposed extended power uprates at Georgia Power’s Hatch Units 1 and 2 (1,832 MW) and Vogtle Units 1 and 2 (2,430 MW). The proposed modifications would add approximately 95 MW at Hatch and 106 MW at Vogtle, increasing generating capacity to 1,927 MW and 2,536 MW, respectively, according to DOE’s project documents. At Hatch, the work would involve replacing the steam dryer, modifying neutron monitoring equipment, and upgrading 16 balance-of-plant systems and components. The Vogtle project entails modifications to 10 balance-of-plant systems, including turbine, feedwater, cooling, and electrical equipment. Georgia Power anticipates submitting NRC license amendment requests for Hatch in the third quarter of 2027 and Vogtle in the fourth quarter of 2028. Both projects remain subject to individual financing reviews under the existing federal loan guarantee agreement.
In September, notably, Georgia Power and Google announced an agreement to support uprates at Hatch and Vogtle that would add approximately 96 MW of nuclear generating capacity. Under the arrangement, Google would subscribe to a proposed nuclear uprate tariff and receive zero-emission credits associated with the additional generation. Georgia Power said the arrangement could provide approximately $900 million in benefits to utility customers over the remaining lives of the reactors, subject to regulatory approval.
UPRISE Identifies 4.7 GW of Potential Nuclear Capacity
In an Oct. 27 fact sheet , DOE said UPRISE has identified approximately 4.7 GW of potential nuclear capacity additions, approaching its 5-GW target for 2029. The program also established an interim target of 2.5 GW by 2027. Although the underlying May 2025 executive order called for 5 GW of uprates at existing reactors, DOE’s current project portfolio also includes the restart of previously retired nuclear plants.
DOE’s fact sheet identifies six major project groups contributing to the reported total:
Constellation Energy: Nearly 1.1 GW of potential uprates at eight facilities, supported by the newly announced conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion.
Vistra: 433 MW of planned uprates at Beaver Valley, Davis-Besse, and Perry, supported by an Oct. 5 conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2 billion.
Southern Co.: More than 300 MW of potential nuclear uprates identified by DOE under its Southern financing program, associated with a $26.5 billion loan package closed in February 2026 that also supports license extensions at Hatch and Farley.
Palisades Nuclear Plant, Michigan: An 800-MW restart supported by a $1.5 billion DOE loan to Holtec.
Crane Clean Energy Center, Pennsylvania: An 835-MW restart supported by $1 billion in DOE financing to Constellation.
Duane Arnold Energy Center, Iowa: A 615-MW restart supported by $1.9 billion in DOE financing to NextEra Energy.
Combined, the three reactor restarts account for approximately 2.25 GW of the identified capacity. However, the six project groups explicitly itemized in DOE’s fact sheet total approximately 4.1 GW, roughly 600 MW short of the agency’s reported 4.7-GW figure. DOE did not explain the difference. The more than 300 MW attributed to Southern also exceeds the approximately 201 MW specified in the September Hatch and Vogtle project documents, although DOE has identified additional future nuclear upgrades under Southern’s financing program.
Project schedules also extend beyond UPRISE’s original milestones: Constellation’s uprates are expected to continue through 2032, while Vistra anticipates completing its projects as late as 2034.
When UPRISE launched in March, former Deputy Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Rian Bahran told POWER that federal engagement was intended to accelerate projects beyond what industry would otherwise accomplish independently. He estimated that DOE’s involvement could enable additional capacity exceeding 1 GW by 2027 and 1 GW by 2029 relative to an industry-only development scenario. Bahran also outlined efforts to address engineering capacity, long-lead equipment procurement, regulatory coordination, and financing, including DOE-facilitated connections between nuclear operators and large electricity customers.
Separately, DOE is also pursuing new nuclear construction through its $17.5 billion American Nuclear Supply Chain Loans initiative, which would finance advance equipment procurement for five eligible projects. The agency said the initiative could accelerate deployment of 10 new reactors by up to three years.
Wright is scheduled to visit Palisades on Oct. 29 as DOE continues to highlight the restart and uprate projects supported by its financing programs.

Ford Is Building a Hypercar With a 5.4-Liter V8 Redlining at 9,000 RPM, but It's Not What You Think
7 photos
Photo: Ford
Yes, Ford is, indeed, working on a hypercar powered by a 5.4-liter V8 engine with naturally aspirated firepower, set to redline at a screaming 9,000 rpm. While the internet is buzzing about a confirmation from Ford, that confirmation did come. But it’s not for a future Mustang-badged, road-legal hypercar.
The rumor mill went into overdrive due to a combination of expectations and leaked clues. While many talk about the potential arrival of a 2027 Boss Mustang with hypercar credentials, Ford has not officially announced a 2027 Boss Mustang production road car.
However, there is a very real and exciting foundation of truth where these rumors are coming from. But the truth is that what Ford is working on around the clock is a Le Mans hypercar. That is what triggered the wave of excitement soon after Ford officially confirmed its 2027 FIA World Endurance Championship (WEC) Hypercar program.
Specifically for this program, Ford is developing a brand-new, naturally aspirated 5.4-liter Coyote-derived V8 engine, specifically to race it at Le Mans . Real-world track testing began over the summer on European circuits, as Ford Racing is making efforts to fine-tune the aerodynamics, hybrid integration, and powertrain.
Photo: Ford Rumors point toward a track-focused dual-clutch automatic transmission that would put power down through the rear wheels in typical Mustang fashion. Yet purists are still dreaming of a Tremec six-speed manual gearbox.
The engine, supposedly making a yet unconfirmed 600 horsepower, was first successfully integrated with its chassis and hybrid system and fired up in July 2026 at ORECA’s facility at the Signes Business Park, right next door to the Circuit Paul Ricard.
Ford also ran the 5.4-liter powerplant on a dyno in Dearborn, simulating a full lap of the Circuit de la Sarthe, where the engine reportedly went past 9,000 rpm. Ford intentionally went for a large-displacement naturally aspirated configuration in order to preserve an aggressive, recognizable American V8 exhaust note on the global endurance stage.
The 5.4-liter V8 powerplant is scheduled to make its official debut in the 2027 FIA World Endurance Championship season, meaning that Ford has a massive development runway to test it throughout what is left of 2026.
Photo: Mustang7G In the meantime, the internet is buzzing with conversations about a potential Ford Mustang with hypercar behavior. An internal document hinting at the 5.4-liter V8 was uploaded in a thread on the Mustang7G Forum, sparking conversation about a potential 2027 Boss Mustang powered by it.
Rumors suggest the arrival of a track-focused Mustang road car, alternatively being referred to by enthusiasts as the "Dark Horse Boss" or code-named "Blackbird," developed to fill the track-day void left by the previous Shelby GT350.
Spy shots of heavily camouflaged Mustang prototypes at the track, featuring advanced corner cooling hardware and a distinct, beefier, high-revving engine note, have been making the rounds, sparking hopes among the Mustang enthusiasts.
For the moment, Ford’s most powerful road car is the GTD , powered by the supercharged 5.2-liter V8, pushing out 815 horsepower (826 metric horsepower).

Bad Sparkplug Put 1964 Pontiac Le Mans out of Service for 47 Years, Full Revival Coming Soon
46 photos
Photo: YouTube/What The Rust?
Finding an unmolested classic from the dawn of the muscle car era is getting to the level where a celebration is in order, that’s how rare of an event it slowly becomes. However, finding rust buckets balances that off perfectly. After all, if the good ones are getting scarcer by the day, it means they either get bad, saved, or scrapped. Well, the ’64 Le Mans recently saved by a couple of wrenching YouTubers is almost all of that.
When a vehicle has spent nearly five decades off the road, expectancy is high about things wrong with it. Richard and Christina Rust of the What the Rust? YouTube channel recently acquired a 1964 Pontiac Le Mans two-door Sport Coupe that had been parked since 1979. After 47 years of silence, the duo set out to revive the machine. Which sounds good (the plan), until they check the car, at which point the plan goes to you-know-where.
Purchased sight unseen after the seller slashed the asking price in half, the Pontiac spent its early life in Fullerton, California, before moving to Tennessee about ten years ago. Because it only saw fifteen years of active road duty in a dry climate, the structural integrity remained in remarkably good condition.
However, 47 years of motionlessness tend to do a number on all the parts that were designed to motion. Like, say, wheels, suspension, engine, transmission, brakes – you get the idea. Even the unloading process proved tricky, as the car lacked both functional brakes and a working Park gear on its transmission selector.
Photo: YouTube/What The Rust? Finished in a pale green repaint applied over silver and the factory green hue, the exterior wears its age with honesty. The sheet metal features original rear quarter panels and a clean roof devoid of vinyl top rust. However, decades under a scorching sun baked the chrome right off the rear bumper, while the front-end misses one headlight bezel and the passenger side bears two noticeable dents in the door and rear quarter.
Rolling on aftermarket Center Line wheels at the rear and temporary 14-inch Chevrolet rollers up front, the Pontiac hides a few oddities underneath. The rear features old air shocks with a leaking air line, and the entire rear brake assembly was mysteriously stripped off decades ago. Inside the cabin, the floor pans are solid in the back and completely shot under the gas pedal, though the rear bench seat, headliner, glovebox, and driver door panel are missing.
The dashboard retains its factory uncut radio bezel, an intact cigarette lighter, and an odometer reading 77,000 miles. I suspect it’s original, meaning whoever had this car put an average of 5,100 miles on it every year. This old Poncho features front bucket seats without a center console, paired with a column-shifted automatic transmission.
Photo: YouTube/What The Rust? While vacuuming the interior, Richard discovered an old key tucked into a corner that operated the door locks and rotated the worn ignition switch. A rusted trunk floor remained the worst non-mechanical flaw on the car.
Popping the hood revealed the dark side of storing a vehicle under a tarp, as trapped moisture had covered the engine bay in heavy surface rust. The car is equipped with the optional 326-cubic-inch (5.3-liter) Pontiac V8, which came completely seized. The radiator was missing, the plastic fan shroud was shattered, and a mud dauber nest had thoroughly plugged the venturis of the two-barrel carburetor. What more could one ask for? Oh, just wait for it.
Richard pulled the old Champion J12Y spark plugs, noting that one plug had carbon bridging the electrode gap, which might have caused a misfire that parked the car in 1979. A borescope inspection showed clean cylinder walls, so he filled all eight cylinders with a 50/50 mixture of acetone and automatic transmission fluid. Checking the dipstick, however, revealed an overfilled crankcase contaminated with clear water.
Photo: YouTube/What The Rust? While the cylinders soaked, he removed the tightly bolted valve covers to find thick black sludge and surface rust across the valvetrain. Using a brass hammer, he tapped the valves to confirm they were bouncing freely and not stuck in their guides. After draining a large volume of what can be best described as” mud” from the oil pan, a breaker bar and cheater pipe on the crankshaft bolt coaxed the 326 V8 into moving.
The next morning, after removing a petrified fan belt fused to the pulleys, Richard worked the crankshaft back and forth until it rotated through a full revolution. However, two hydraulic lifters were stuck in the raised position due to heavy sludge buildup. Pouring diesel fuel directly into the lifter valley and tapping the components freed the stubborn lifters, restoring tension and movement across all 16 rockers.
Removing the oil pan drain plug again unleashed thick, gelatinous chunks of black sludge that required prodding with a screwdriver to clear. To clean the internal passages, Richard poured six dollars’ worth of diesel fuel into the crankcase for a multi-stage flush, repeating the process three times before refilling with fresh motor oil. He also freed up a dry, seized power steering pump and cleaned the carburetor in an ultrasonic bath.
Photo: YouTube/What The Rust? With the rear axle placed safely on jack stands to prevent the misaligned transmission linkage from engaging gear, it was time to test the electrical system. Jumping the starter trigger wire at the horn relay confirmed the starter motor was functional. After replacing a faulty negative battery cable, cleaning oil-fouled spark plugs, and giving the intake a shot of starting fluid, the engine began to detonate.
Adjusting the distributor timing twice proved to be the magic touch. On the next crank, the 326 V8 roared to life for the first time in 47 years, building oil pressure and belching thick clouds of white and black smoke from the tailpipe. It ran briefly off the fuel bowl before stalling, proving that the vintage Pontiac heart was still viable despite its noisy valvetrain.
To run the engine longer, the cooling system needed water, which led to the discovery of a rusted thermostat housing and a blown freeze plug leaking behind the starter. Furthermore, one rocker arm remained exceptionally loose despite a straight pushrod and an uncollapsed lifter. Richard pulled the pushrods, cleared their clogged internal oil passages with wire, and reassembled the top end.
Photo: YouTube/What The Rust? On the final startup, the cleaned pushrods transformed the engine's behavior, quieting the clatter and allowing the Pontiac to settle into a shaky idle. With a replacement freeze plug, a carburetor float adjustment, and a long fan belt still needed, the rescue paused on a triumphant note, proving this 1964 seven-piston V8 survivor is ready for a second lease on life.
Named after the famous 24-hour endurance race in France, the Pontiac Le Mans moniker debuted in late 1961 as a sporty, upscale trim package on the compact Tempest line. Featuring bucket seats and distinctive badging, it occupied the top tier of the Tempest hierarchy through 1963 before transitioning onto the newly enlarged intermediate A-body platform for 1964, where it famously spawned the GTO performance option.
Production figures across the years reflect the shifting tides of the American automotive market. During the first generation, Pontiac built 7,455 Tempest Le Mans coupes in 1961, jumping to 55,221 units in 1962 (39,662 coupes and 15,559 convertibles) and 61,658 units in 1963. Entering the intermediate era, total Le Mans output reached 108,630 units in 1964 (including GTOs), 182,905 in 1965, 135,967 in 1966, and 104,902 in 1967.
Photo: YouTube/What The Rust? The 1964 Le Mans was offered two-door body styles riding on a 115-inch wheelbase: Sport Coupe (post), pillarless hardtop, and convertible. Excluding the 32,450 GTO-optioned cars, regular Le Mans production totaled 76,180 units. The hardtops were the hotcakes, with 31,310 copies sold (plus another 18,422 GTOs). Most of them came with V8 power (23,901).
Under the hood, the standard 1964 Le Mans powerplant was a 215-cubic-inch (3.5-liter) inline 6-cylinder rated at 140 horsepower at 4,400 rpm. Buyers wanting V8 power could step up to the 326-cubic-inch Pontiac V8, offered with an 8.6:1 compression ratio and a two-barrel carburetor making 250 horsepower, or a 10.5:1 High Output single-quad version delivering 280 horsepower. Checking the 295-dollar GTO option unlocked the 389-cubic-inch V8 with 325 horsepower (four-barrel) or 348 horsepower (Tri-Power).
Transmission choices for 1964 began with a standard column-shifted 3-speed manual, while optional gearboxes included a floor-shifted 3-speed heavy-duty manual, a Muncie 4-speed manual (available in wide-ratio or close-ratio configurations), and the 2-speed TempesTorque automatic transmission.

source_document.body:
Executives from Werner Enterprises outlined a path to double-digit truckload margins, but said cost headwinds will likely limit progress over the next two quarters.
Werner ( NASDAQ: WERN ) reported third-quarter adjusted earnings per share of 16 cents after the market closed on Tuesday. The result was in line with a profit warning issued earlier in the month, calling for adjusted EPS of 15 to 16 cents versus the 36-cent consensus estimate at the time.
Consolidated revenue of $951 million was 23% higher year over year and at the top end of management’s revised outlook ($946 million to $951 million). The increase was largely due to higher fuel surcharges and the January acquisition of dedicated carrier FirstFleet.
Table: Werner’s key performance indicators
EPS bridge from Q3 to Q4
Sequential cost increases from elevated diesel fuel prices, higher driver procurement expenses and a reserve adjustment for prior claims were an 18-cent EPS drag on the third quarter. Gains on asset sales increased y/y from $4.5 million to $8 million, providing a 4-cent tailwind. (The company booked an adjusted net loss of 3 cents per share in the 2025 third quarter.)
Werner said some costs, like driver recruiting and training, were front-loaded expenses incurred ahead of a revenue offset. For instance, it had to bear the costs of adding 130 dedicated trucks and drivers throughout the quarter, even though the revenue stream didn’t begin until the end of the period.
“We made the deliberate decision to accelerate investments in driver recruiting and onboarding to capture rising customer demand and support fleet expansion as industry capacity tightens,” said Chairman and CEO Derek Leathers. “We remain confident in our trajectory and our ability to capitalize on the early stages of this freight upcycle.”
However, it also said some cost headwinds will linger into the first quarter.
It provided a soft guide for “modest sequential [EPS] improvement” in the fourth quarter (from the 16-cent result in the third quarter). But the result will probably be materially below the current 38-cent fourth-quarter consensus estimate.
Approximately one third of the 18-cent third-quarter EPS drag was tied to driver recruiting and sign-on bonuses, and does not represent “structural labor inflation,” management said. The remaining 12 cents stemmed from fuel and insurance claims, which should largely dissipate in the fourth quarter. However, lower gains on sale (guided to total just $1.7 million), higher interest expense and a higher tax rate are additional headwinds. Better pricing and a slightly larger fleet to accommodate peak season demand will provide some offsets.
Truckload fuel surcharges operate on a one-week lag. Diesel prices were up sequentially in nine of the 13 weeks of the third quarter. By month, retail diesel prices dipped 1% sequentially in July, but increased 10% sequentially in August and another 15% in September. The near-term headwind will become an earnings tailwind when diesel prices revert.
Other Q3 takeaways
The company’s dedicated segment (81% of its total truck fleet) reported a 52% y/y increase in revenue (ex-fuel) as the average truck count was up 44% y/y to nearly 7,000 units and revenue per truck per week (ex-fuel) increased 6% y/y. (The FirstFleet deal added over 2,400 tractors and $615 million in annual revenue.)
Dedicated revenue per truck per week is now expected to increase by 4 to 5% y/y for full-year 2026, an increase from the prior outlook for a 3-to-5% increase.
The one-way unit again saw big gains in utilization following a restructuring earlier in the year, which included exiting non-profitable accounts and repurposing under-utilized equipment. One-way revenue was down 15% y/y (ex-fuel) as the average truck count declined 37% y/y. Revenue per truck per week (ex-fuel) increased 34% y/y as miles per truck increased 22% and revenue per total mile (ex-fuel) increased 10%. The rate-per-mile metric was negatively impacted by a 116-mile increase in length of haul. (Longer hauls usually accompany lower per-mile rates.)
SONAR: Van Contract Rate Per Mile Index ( VCRPM1.USA ) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). The index shows a 7-day moving average of the initial reporting of dry van contract rates without fuel or accessorial charges. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
Guidance for the one-way fleet again calls for a 10-to-13% y/y increase in revenue per total mile during the fourth quarter. Roughly 60% of the one-way revenue book renews in the first half of 2027. Management is eyeing double-digit increases on many of these renewals.
One-way saw more than 800 basis points of y/y margin improvement in the quarter (actual margin not disclosed). Werner is again looking to grow this fleet.
The TL unit recorded $714 million in combined revenue, a 37% y/y increase (up 28% y/y excluding fuel surcharges). A 95.9% adjusted operating ratio (4.1% adjusted operating margin) was 220 bps better y/y, but 140 bps worse than the prior quarter . Management said the sequential cost headwinds represented a 200-bp drag.
The company’s logistics unit reported a 7% y/y revenue decline to $216 million, but returned to profitability, posting a 0.4% adjusted operating margin. Truckload brokerage, which operates within the logistics unit, booked 600 bps of sequential operating margin improvement. (Werner does not disclose this subsegment’s margin results.)
Why it matters? Werner’s third-quarter result shows the significant cost pressures carriers are currently facing—specifically rising diesel fuel prices and higher driver procurement costs. It signals that the industry’s recovery following will not be linear, and that while carriers are raising rates, profitability is still being squeezed by early-upcycle cost inflation.

Photo: Ørsted
Over the coming year, renewables’ share of total generating capacity will grow from 37.7% to 40.4%, surpassing that of natural gas and outstripping nuclear capacity fivefold, according to new data released by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and reviewed by the SUN DAY Campaign.
Renewable electricity generation grew by more than 10% over the past year
According to the EIA’s latest “ Electric Power Monthly ” report (with data through August 31, 2026), renewably generated electricity during the first two-thirds of 2026 was 10.2% greater year over year. The growth was led by utility-scale [>1 MW] solar (up 20.0%), small-scale solar (up 12.0%), wind (up 7.8%), hydropower (up 4.2%), and geothermal (up 3.8%).
From January to August 2026, wind produced 333,367 gigawatt-hours (GWh) – 10.6% of total US electrical generation – while utility-scale and small-scale solar combined produced 329,119 GWh (10.5%), hydropower produced 180,940 GWh (5.7%), biomass produced 29,917 GWh (1.0%), and geothermal produced 10,766 GWh (0.34%).
By comparison, the electrical output of US natural gas and nuclear power plants grew more slowly – by just 2.6% and 1.3%, respectively. Electricity produced by US coal plants fell by 8.7%.

During the first eight months of 2026, the combination of wind and solar, including small-scale solar, accounted for almost 21.1% of domestic electricity production, with wind at 10.6% and solar at nearly 10.5%.
During the first two-thirds of this year, wind and solar combined produced 44.4% more electricity than coal and 24.8% more than nuclear.
Through the end of August, the mix of all renewables, including biomass, accounted for 28.1% of total US electrical generation – up from 26.2% a year earlier.
Over the past year, renewable energy capacity increased by over 43,000 MW
Between September 1, 2025, and August 31, 2026, the installed capacity of utility-scale solar increased by 27,141.7 MW, while that of small-scale solar and wind grew by 6,526.1 MW and 9,979.1 MW (including 800 MW of offshore wind), respectively. The combined capacity of all renewable energy sources, including hydropower, biomass, and geothermal, expanded by 43,497.9 MW.
In addition, utility-scale battery energy storage capacity increased by 17,586.9 MW.
By comparison, coal capacity fell by 2,703.4 MW, while nuclear capacity remained unchanged. However, natural gas capacity rose by 5,316.0 MW. Combined, net new nuclear and fossil fuel capacity totaled just 2,612.6 MW.
Thus, renewable energy’s capacity expansion was nearly 17 times greater than the net growth of fossil fuels and nuclear power combined.
Utility-scale renewables to add over 53 GW of new capacity in the coming year
The EIA projects that the rapid growth of renewables over the past year will accelerate in the coming year.
As of September 1, 2026, renewable energy’s share of total US utility-scale generating capacity was 34.5%. EIA projects this to grow to 37.3% by August 31, 2027. Utility-scale solar will add 44,603.1 MW, thereby expanding its share from 13.4% to 16.5%, while wind will grow by 8,312.3 MW (including 3,355.0 MW of offshore wind), increasing from 13.4% to 13.5%. The mix of other renewables (hydropower, biomass, and geothermal) will add 201.9 MW.
The combined net capacity growth of all utility-scale renewable energy sources over the 12-month period (53,117.3 MW) is almost 44% higher than that added over the previous 12 months (36,971.8 MW). It would bring renewables’ share of total US utility-scale generating capacity up to 37.3%.
Meanwhile, EIA projects no new nuclear generating capacity and a net decline of 1,997.0 MW in fossil fuel capacity.
With new small-scale solar, renewables’ capacity is on track to surpass natural gas by summer 2027
The figures cited above don’t include small-scale solar. The estimated capacity of small-scale solar systems grew by 6,526.1 MW during the last year, bringing its total to 63,192.6 MW. EIA does not provide a forecast for small-scale solar capacity growth over the next 12 months, but the SUN DAY Campaign assumes it will roughly equal the 6,400 MW added on average over each of the past five years. Therefore, it is conservatively assumed that an additional 6,000 MW or more will come online in the coming year.
If small-scale solar increases by approximately 6,000 MW by September 1, 2027, it will bring renewable energy’s installed capacity to about 550,000 MW. By comparison, natural gas’ projected generating capacity would total 518,312.8 MW.
Solar power’s share alone would be more than one-fifth (20.7%) of total US generating capacity.
Battery storage to increase by almost 44% by next September
EIA foresees battery energy storage adding another 23,656.2 MW by September 1, 2027 – an increase of 43.7%, bringing the total up to 77,753.2 MW.
Thus, the combination of utility-scale renewable energy sources and battery energy storage will provide 76,773.5 MW of new clean energy capacity by late summer 2027. With the inclusion of small-scale solar, that figure could rise to 82.8 GW of new generating capacity.
“Each new issue of EIA’s ‘Electric Power Monthly’ reinforces the theme that the growth of solar, wind, and battery storage has become unstoppable,” noted the SUN DAY Campaign’s executive director Ken Bossong. “Meanwhile, the share of the nation’s electrical generation and generating capacity provided by fossil fuels and nuclear continues to shrink.”

Owner Paid $133,770 for This Rare-Color Porsche and Passed Away. His Car Just Sold for $141,300
25 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
Sometimes, just sometimes, cars laugh in the face of depreciation. And always, just always, they have something that makes their value skyrocket over the years. That’s the story with this 2023 Porsche 718 Boxster Spyder, acquired for $133,770 in 2023 and sold soon after the owner passed away for $7,530 more in 2026. The ace up its sleeve? The Gold Bronze Metallic paint.
Bye-bye, MSRP! Hello Paint-to-Sample Gold Bronze Metallic. That is one rare paint that drastically changes the sticker price of the model or its value on the used car market. For the 2023 model year in the United States, checking the box for a standard Paint-to-Sample color like the Gold Bronze Metallic added an extra $11,430 to the vehicle’s build sheet.
That was on top of the MSRP of $103,400 before any destination fees or before checking any option boxes. Because the daring Gold Bronze Metallic paint code Z52 is exceptionally rare on the 718, cars with that finish are highly coveted by collectors. Such cars frequently command between $130,000 and $150,000 on auction platforms.
Porsche built a total of 7,955 718 Boxster Spyders across its entire production run between 2020 and 2023. Only 1,365 units were built globally for the 2023 model year, with just 426 allocated to North America. Paint-to-Sample allocations were very expensive and difficult to secure during the final model year.
Photo: Cars and Bids Sporting a generous amount of metallic flake, the paint finish leans more toward bronze than actual gold. Under direct bright sunlight, it displays a radiant golden-yellow base, deep copper undertones, and even a silver sheen. In overcast conditions, it pulls back into a sophisticated light-bronze tone.
The unconventional color debuted in 2010 on the ultra-limited 997-generation 911 Turbo S 10th Anniversary Edition , which was produced exclusively for the Chinese market. Only ten examples saw the light of day back then.
It was later added to Porsche’s Paint-to-Sample ultra-exclusive catalog via a special PTS Plus customer request. Only a handful of 718 Spyders in the world were ever painted in the show-stopping Z52 finish that is called Goldbronzemetallic in its home market, Germany.
In the meantime, Porsche discontinued the Gold Bronze Metallic, locking it away as an option only available for the Macan and the Panamera, which makes the 2023 Porsche 718 Boxster Spyder the more exclusive. The bronze-gold Porsche rides on 20-inch wheels finished in Satin Platinum with tires date-coded 2022.
Photo: Cars and Bids This car is not all show and no go. The 718 Boxster is powered by Porsche’s 4.0-liter flat-six with naturally aspirated firepower, pushing out 414 horsepower (420 metric horsepower) and 309 pound-feet (420 Newton meters) of torque when the manual transmission is involved, which is the case for this car.
That six-speed manual transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 4.2 seconds, a quarter mile in 12.0 seconds with a trap speed of 118 mph (190 kph), and a top speed of 187 mph (301 kph).
The owner, however, did not enjoy those much. He bought it brand-new back in March 2023, paying $133,770 to drive it home. He passed away earlier this year, and the estate sold his Porsche with only 4,013 miles (6,458 kilometers) on the clock. " There was no reason to sell the car other than the owner has unfortunately passed ," the estate representative explained.
The bidding took off in the final minutes, reaching an incredible $141,300, which is far above the average. classic.com claims the average price for a 2023 Porsche 718 Boxster Spyder is around $118,780.
Photo: Cars and Bids The seller says the car has never been tracked and has never been driven in winter, but was PPF-ed from bumper to bumper at the dealer, even before it was first driven, which means the eye-catching paint underneath should be intact. The car is still under warranty until March 20, 2027.
The gold-painted body and the manual black soft top shelter a cabin in black leather and Race-Tex upholstery with contrasting red stitching. The theme extends to the dashboard and door panels. Heated seats and carbon fiber trim are also on board.
A Burmester High-End surround sound system provides the soundtrack on board when the driver has had enough of the Boxster orchestra, as if that can ever happen. The owner had an aftermarket exhaust valve remote control system for more drama.
The buyer is taking home a car with a clean Carfax, two keys, the owner’s manual, the window sticker, and a battery tender. His car is ready to drive. The engine oil and filter, along with the air filter and spark plugs, were replaced in March 2026 at 3,760 miles (6,051 kilometers).
From this moment on, the new owner has two options: store the car in a climate-controlled garage, sit and watch how its value goes through the roof over the years, or drive it until its wheels fall off. Either way, he is a winner.
